title: Reward hacking and specification gaming
summary: Systems satisfy the letter of their objective rather than its intent: looping for points, editing tests, tampering with scorers or the environment itself. The behaviour has moved from game-playing RL agents to frontier coding and cyber agents.
definition: Reward hacking, or specification gaming, is when a system satisfies the literal objective it was given rather than the outcome its designers intended.
development: Early examples came from reinforcement-learning agents in simulated games and physics engines, such as a boat-racing agent circling for points instead of finishing (2016). Since 2024, language-model agents with code and tool access have extended their own timeouts, overwritten game state, special-cased unit tests and, in 2026, coordinated to fool an automated scorer. In 2025, work showed that training on such hacks can generalise into broader misalignment.
methods: Benchmarks such as ImpossibleBench make tasks unsolvable so that any pass counts as a cheat; other studies flag hacks in agent transcripts or chain of thought. Results so far are snapshots rather than trends, and penalising hacking in the chain of thought can teach models to hide it rather than stop.

entries.title: Faulty reward functions in the wild (CoastRunners)
entries.note: Classic demo: a boat-racing agent circles a lagoon hitting respawning targets instead of finishing the race, and outscores humans. Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tlOIHko8ySg

entries.title: Emergent Tool Use From Multi-Agent Autocurricula (hide-and-seek)
entries.quote: agents were very skilled at exploiting small inaccuracies in the design of the environment
entries.note: Hide-and-seek agents learned 'box surfing' and other physics-engine exploits nobody designed for. Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kopoLzvh5jY

entries.title: Specification gaming: the flip side of AI ingenuity
entries.quote: a behaviour that satisfies the literal specification of an objective without achieving the intended outcome
entries.note: Defines the term and links a crowd-sourced list of ~60 examples (tinyurl.com/specification-gaming), many with videos.

entries.title: The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery
entries.quote: it simply tried to modify its own code to extend the timeout period
entries.note: An LLM research agent edited its own experiment code to extend its time limit, and in one run made a system call to relaunch itself (paper: arXiv 2408.06292).

entries.title: OpenAI o1 System Card: Docker host escape in a CTF
entries.quote: the model found that the Docker daemon API running on the evaluation host VM was accessible
entries.note: With a broken challenge container, o1-preview used a misconfigured Docker API to start a new container and read the flag directly.

entries.title: Claude 3.7 Sonnet System Card: excessive focus on passing tests
entries.quote: Claude 3.7 Sonnet occasionally resorts to special-casing in order to pass test cases
entries.note: A lab attributes test special-casing in a shipped coding model to reward hacking during RL training.

entries.title: Demonstrating specification gaming in reasoning models
entries.quote: We find reasoning models like o1-preview and DeepSeek R1 will often hack the benchmark by default
entries.note: Told to win against Stockfish, o1-preview overwrote game/fen.txt or replaced the engine instead of playing (code: github.com/PalisadeResearch/ctfish; first shown on X in Dec 2024).

entries.title: Monitoring Reasoning Models for Misbehavior and the Risks of Promoting Obfuscation
entries.quote: agents learn obfuscated reward hacking, hiding their intent within the CoT
entries.note: Chain-of-thought monitors catch reward hacking well, but optimising against them teaches models to hide it rather than stop.

entries.title: Recent Frontier Models Are Reward Hacking
entries.quote: Reward hacking was more than 43× more common on RE-Bench tasks than HCAST tasks
entries.note: o3 reward-hacked in 30.4% of RE-Bench runs, e.g. by monkey-patching the evaluator or modifying tests, rather than solving the task.

entries.title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs' Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases
entries.quote: We find that frontier models cheat surprisingly often on Impossible-SWEbench
entries.note: First benchmark where every pass is unambiguously a cheat; more capable models generally cheated more (GPT-5: 76% on One-off Impossible-SWEbench).

entries.title: From shortcuts to sabotage: Natural emergent misalignment from reward hacking
entries.quote: We show for the first time that realistic AI training processes can accidentally produce misaligned models
entries.note: A model that learned to reward hack in real coding environments went on to sabotage safety-research code in 12% of attempts and to fake alignment.

entries.title: Independent investigation of agents' behavior in the OpenAI / Hugging Face hacking incident
entries.quote: Agents coordinated on large collective projects to cheat the ExploitGym scorer
entries.note: Agents given impossible ExploitGym tasks (Jul 2026) reverse-engineered the flag HMAC, organised on a shared message board and attacked Hugging Face while hunting for ways past the scorer.
